publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Adequately to discuss the vast and fascinating subject opened up by Mr. Pask in his paper would require more time than the programme of this evening permits, but I cannot allow the opportunity to pass of adding my support to Mr. Pask's proposal that this Institute should interest itself in the collection and study of data on phenomena of such immediate and engrossing importance to a large proportion of the membership. I said “proposal.” Mr. Pask's appeal, however, is rather a clarion call reminding us of our obligations to the Institute and to the scientists and engineers in other parts of the world, from whom we have been content, in large measure, to take, and to whom, in our turn, we have not given in the same degree. We do not possess, of course, the large undertakings, factories, and universities, nor the financial facilities of Europe and America, and all these points are duly recognised by Mr. Pask; in fact, his paper may be said fairly to hold the balance between scientific enthusiasm and a recognition of practical facts. Nevertheless, after making due allowance for every limiting factor which must place a curb on our ambition, there is no doubt but that a certain modest amount of work can be done by this Institute with immediate benefit to numbers of our fellow citizens. I refer to the dissemination of information, in such form as to be easily understood and applied, on lightning conductors and the prevention of fatal accidents during lightning storms. A small pamphlet could be made available to architects, builders, and the public at the cost of printing, and, doubtless, the Department of Native Affairs could be persuaded to undertake the task of spreading the most important information amongst the natives. articleTitle: Boiler-house load equalisation
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The vast majority of steam generating plants have to deal with steam-using equipment, the demand of which varies from hour to hour, minute to minute, or even from second to second. The transference of the steam demand, unaltered, to the steam generating section of the plant imposes a duty on the latter which is frequently very severe, and which seldom permits of the boilers operating at their best efficiency, not to mention the strain placed on the operating staff in many instances. The desirability of approximating as closely as possible to constant-firing conditions, maintained over longish periods of time, is almost self-evident, and this is the object aimed at in what I have termed Boiler-house Load Equalisation.

abstract: I shall have the honour to demonstrate to you to-night a few of the more important features having hearing on the design of modern oil switches in general, and on the Brown-Boveri oil switch in particular. Some repetitions, however, are unavoidable, but as the conclusions in some respects deviate from the views previously expressed, I trust my paper may prove of interest.

articleTitle: “Entropy from a thermo-dynamical standpoint”
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Every practical engineer has a very sound notion of the significance and application of the more ordinary units of heat-used in thermodynamics and he applies them freely and knowledgeably in his daily calculations. There is, however, one unit which he uses just as freely, and which he finds extremely useful in his work, but which, as a rule, he is quite unable to visualise. This is the unit of entropy. It has always shown itself to be a stumbling block to students in the study of thermodynamics, and many operating engineers have but a faint understanding of this somewhat elusive quantity. It is, of course, not necessary that they should be conversant with its derivation so long as they can employ it intelligently in their work, but, nevertheless, an appreciative conception of this quantity must, without doubt, give an added interest to their problems and possibly open up other fields for its application. The engineer who is desirous of widening his knowledge upon this subject opens up his heat engine textbook under the heading “Entropy,” and finds, to his disappointment, that the definition given is very cursory and far from illuminating.

articleTitle: Presidential address
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: In expressing to you my great appreciation of the honour the members of this Institute have conferred upon me in choosing me to be their President for the current year, I would assure you that while I am deeply sensible of your kindness and confidence, I am very mindful of the responsibilities which the high office entails. Doubtless many of you will remember the anxieties which beset the Council of this Institute only a few years ago when it seemed as if its activities were vain and that its days of usefulness were drawing to a close. Those worrying days have passed, we all hope for ever, and the name of the Institute to-day stands as high as it probably has at any period in its history. Bearing in mind that its present fortunes and high position are largely due to the able leadership and the untiring energy of its Presidents of the past years, I approach the office to winch you have elected me with a full realisation of the onerous, but to me extremely pleasant, duties which it entails.

publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Overall power economy can be improved in two directions: First, by aiming at steadiness in production, and, secondly, by steadiness in consumption. The demand of energy (heat and power) can be controlled, to a certain extent, in self-contained industries (textile and paper factories, steel works and sugar factories), but in most cases no appreciable advantages are obtainable without danger to the process of manufacture. In the electric supply business no control is possible; all that can be done is to influence consumers by means of the tariff.

articleTitle: An introduction to discussion on lead accumulators
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: It was with interest I read the paper by Mr. Keller introducing a discussion on lead accumulators, and I think a word of congratulation is due to the author for introducing this very important but neglected electrical engineering unit. Batteries have failed after a few years of service through, in a majority of instances, ignorance and neglect, and I have often heard engineers say that they would not have a battery in the place, as it is too much trouble to look after them, I would like to outline from my point of view what I consider some of the most important points in the maintenance of a battery, I am not going to touch on the technical and chemical details, but more or less try and deal with some of the practical points for maintenance. The most important point to my way of thinking is the steps to be taken when a battery is to be installed new. On the question of erection, in the majority of instances the details are supplied by the makers, detailing the stands, insulators, separators, etc. The battery may be well fitted together, and its electrical connections may be all that is desired, but when this is all done the point is, and the most important point is, what is put into the battery in the way of acid and water. One cannot emphasize too much the correct chemical contents of these two items. If proper attention is not given in the smallest detail to the correct electrolyte, then the battery must suffer in the years to come, and no matter how careful one may be after, the battery is sure to suffer should any trace of iron, etc., be left in the electrolyte.

abstract: I wish to take this opportunity of thanking the President and Council for the opportunity of addressing the members of the Institute on the work of the “Saela” Lighting Service Bureau and the subject of Illumination. Possibly some electrical engineers may question the advisability of the presentation of two papers on the subject within five months, but I can assure you that throughout the world the question of the scientific application of illuminating engineering is at present receiving the greatest attention, and where there has been acute industrial depression the supply authorities have found that improved lighting can absorb the major part of the lost industrial load; in fact, during the past four years, the larger cities in Europe and America have seen an almost undreamt of transformation in the use of electric lighting.

abstract: The paper by Mr. Keller is an introduction to a very interesting subject, but I don't think most of us appreciate how interesting it is. abstract: Honours and privileges are usually expected to carry with them corresponding obligations and responsibilities. It seems to have become a traditional obligation for the President of the Associated Scientific and Technical Societies of South Africa to deliver a valedictory address, reviewing the more important work done during his year of office, and sometimes advising the incoming President regarding certain matters that should be considered by the new Council. The Annual Report gives a concise statement of the work done and results obtained during last year; in some instances, particularly in the representations to certain government departments, the results appear meagre, but on the whole a measure of success has been achieved.

articleTitle: British engineering standards association
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The British Engineering Standards Association has recently issued a revision of British Standard Specification No. 91 electric cable soldering sockets for cables from 0.003 to 1 sq. in. sectional area. The design and dimensions of cast and tubular sockets have not been altered as compared with the previous edition of the specification, but an important modification has been made in that hot-pressed sockets are now recognised as standard, whereas formerly cast sockets and tubular sockets were the only types recognised as standard. The material for the manufacture of hot-pressed sockets is specified, as are also the dimensions. A useful feature of the revised specification is the insertion of tables giving the approximate current (at the Institute Electrical Engineer's rating) of the largest conductor for which the different sizes of socket is suitable. A new appendix has been added to the specification, giving the International Standards of resistance for copper.
